To corrupt something or someone means to take what was originally good, pure, honest, or working correctly — and damage or change it so that it becomes bad, dishonest, or broken.

The most important thing to understand is the direction of this change: it always goes from good → bad, or from correct → wrong. The word carries the idea that something fell from a better state into a worse one. Something outside (or sometimes inside) caused that fall.

A simple mental image: picture a clean glass of water. Now imagine someone slowly drips poison into it. The water goes from pure to contaminated. Whatever caused that — and the process itself — is what "corrupt" describes. The water didn't start out poisoned. It was made that way.
The Three Main Ways "Corrupt" Is Used

1. Corrupting a Person — Morally and Ethically

This is the most powerful and common use of the word. When a person is corrupted, they are made dishonest, immoral, or wicked — usually after having been decent or good. Something acts on them and slowly changes who they are.

A young, idealistic judge enters the legal system with a genuine desire for justice. Over years, criminals offer him money, favors, and threats. Slowly, he starts bending the rules — first a little, then a lot. His values, his integrity, and his honesty have all been corrupted. He is not the same person he once was. Something changed him.

What does the corrupting? The cause can be:

  • Greed ("Greed corrupted him beyond recognition.")
  • Power ("Absolute power corrupts absolutely." — one of the most famous sayings in the English language, meaning: the more power a person has, the more likely they are to become dishonest and self-serving.)
  • Bad influences ("The people he surrounded himself with eventually corrupted him.")
  • Bribery ("The crime syndicate corrupted dozens of local officials with cash payments.")
  • Flattery, comfort, or temptation of any kind

Notice that in all these cases, the person usually wasn't corrupt before. The word implies a fall — a change from better to worse.

2. Corrupting Data or a File — In Technology

In computers and digital systems, to corrupt a file or data means to damage or alter it so that it can no longer be read correctly, opened properly, or used the way it was intended.

"The sudden power cut corrupted all the files on my hard drive." This means the files were damaged internally — not deleted, but broken in a way that makes them unusable.

What does the corrupting in technology?

  • A computer virus ("The virus corrupted the operating system.")
  • A sudden power failure
  • A software bug or error
  • A failed download or transfer

The key idea is the same as with people: something that was functioning correctly has been changed into something broken or unreadable. The content or structure inside has been altered in a harmful way.

3. Corrupting a Text or Information

A written document, a historical record, a message, or any piece of information can be corrupted — meaning its original, accurate content has been changed, distorted, or damaged so that it no longer reflects the truth or the original.

"After centuries of being copied by hand, the original manuscript was severely corrupted." This means that generations of scribes made errors, introduced changes, or mistranslated words — so what we read today is no longer what the original author actually wrote. The text drifted away from its true form.

"Bias corrupted the findings of the study." Here, prejudice changed the data or conclusions so that they no longer accurately reflect reality.
The Structure of the Verb: Who Does What to Whom

"Corrupt" is a transitive verb. This is a grammar term that simply means: the verb always needs an object — it always acts on something or someone. You don't just corrupt; you corrupt something.

The basic pattern is: [cause] + corrupts + [person or thing]

  • Power corrupts leaders.
  • The malware corrupted the system.
  • Living in that world corrupted his sense of right and wrong.

It is also very commonly used in the passive voice — where the focus shifts to what was affected, rather than what caused it:

  • The files were corrupted during the crash.
  • He was corrupted by years of working alongside dishonest people.
  • The original message has been corrupted in transmission.

In the passive form, the cause may not even be mentioned. The emphasis is simply on the fact that the thing is now in a damaged or degraded state.

When "corrupt" is used about people and moral character, it almost always describes a slow process. Corruption rarely happens in a single moment. A person doesn't go from honest to deeply dishonest overnight. The word carries the feel of a slow rot — like rust forming on metal, or mold spreading through food. Day by day, the original goodness is eaten away until something different remains.

This is why you will often see words like "slowly," "gradually," or "over time" used alongside it in this context:

  • "The system slowly corrupted even those who entered it with pure intentions."
  • "Years of unchecked power had gradually corrupted his judgment."

In technology, however, corruption can be instantaneous — a file can be corrupted in a split second.
What Makes "Corrupt" Different from Simply "Break" or "Damage"

Not all harm is corruption. The word is precise. To corrupt something means to alter it from within — to change its nature, its purity, or its correctness — rather than simply destroying it from the outside.

If you smash a computer with a hammer, you've broken it. But if a virus secretly enters it and rewrites its code, you've corrupted it. The machine might still appear to function — but something inside has been secretly, deeply changed for the worse.

This same idea applies to people. A person who is physically harmed has not been corrupted. But a person whose values, honesty, and character have been secretly changed by greed or power has been corrupted — they may still look and act normal, but something fundamental inside them has shifted.

Corruption, then, is about internal degradation from a once-good state — not simply about breakage or destruction.

These are words and phrases that frequently appear together with "corrupt" in real usage:

  • Power corrupts — probably the most famous use of this verb in English
  • Corrupt someone with [money / bribes / gifts / flattery] — to cause someone to become dishonest by tempting them
  • Corrupt the youth — a centuries-old phrase meaning to lead young people toward immoral thinking or behavior
  • Corrupt data / corrupt a file — to damage digital information
  • Corrupt an official / corrupt a judge — to cause a person in authority to act dishonestly, usually through bribery
  • Corrupt the truth — to distort or misrepresent what is true
  • Corrupt the mind — to fill a person's thinking with harmful or dishonest ideas

• "Living in that environment for so long slowly corrupted his values." (moral use)
  • "She tried to corrupt the witness by offering him a large sum of money to lie in court." (bribery use)
  • "The software crash corrupted several important documents on my computer." (technology use)
  • "It is often said that money and fame will corrupt even the most principled people." (general moral use)
  • "Centuries of poor translation and careless copying have corrupted the original meaning of the text." (text/information use)
  • "He allowed himself to be corrupted — no one forced him into it." (showing the person had some agency)
  • "Absolute power corrupts absolutely." (the famous saying)

To corrupt means: to take something that was good, pure, honest, or correctly functioning — and, through an outside or inside force, change or damage it so deeply that it becomes bad, dishonest, impure, or broken.

The thing doing the corrupting is usually something powerful: greed, power, a bribe, a virus, bias, or a bad influence. The thing being corrupted usually started out in a good or proper state. And the result of corruption is always a degraded, spoiled, or altered version of what something — or someone — once was.
